issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette: Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a bomb disposal technician. He had spent decades defusing explosives and saving lives, earning him a reputation as one of the best in the business. But it was on a fateful day five years ago that everything changed. Kofi's team was called to dispose of a toxic chemical leak at a manufacturing plant. As they worked to contain the spill, Kofi was exposed to a lethal dose of the chemical. He remembers feeling a searing pain in his lungs and a creeping numbness in his extremities. In the aftermath of the incident, Kofi began to notice that certain smells would transport him back to that day. The antiseptic scent of hospitals, in particular, made him feel like he was reliving the exposure all over again. He started avoiding medical appointments and would become anxious whenever his wife, Ama, suggested they visit a doctor. Loud noises also became a trigger for Kofi's anxiety; the sound of sirens or explosions would send his heart racing, making him feel like he was in imminent danger. As time went on, Kofi found ways to cope with these triggers by avoiding situations that might set them off. He stopped going to his favorite coffee shop because it was too close to the hospital and instead started working from home. But being alone in a room or building made him feel uneasy, so he began taking on more projects at work, often clocking 12-hour shifts just to avoid being by himself. His wife would sometimes complain that she never saw him anymore, but Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling of restlessness when he was idle. Kofi also developed a habit of scanning his surroundings for potential dangers. He would scope out escape routes whenever he entered a new room or building, mentally mapping out the safest exit in case of an emergency. His friends and family started to notice that he seemed more on edge than usual, always looking over his shoulder as if expecting something to go wrong. One day, while Ama was trying to give him a hug, Kofi recoiled in surprise. She asked what was wrong, but all he could say was that he just wasn't used to being touched anymore. It wasn't just physical touch that made him jumpy; even unexpected noises or movements would startle him. As the months went by, Kofi's behaviors started to take a toll on his relationships and daily life. His overwork began to affect his performance at work, causing friction with his colleagues. Ama felt like she was losing her husband to this new, anxious version of himself. She pleaded with him to seek help, but Kofi was convinced that he could manage on his own. It wasn't until a recent incident at work, where Kofi had a panic attack in response to a loud noise, that he realized he needed assistance. His colleagues staged an intervention, urging him to get professional help before things escalated further. With Ama's support, Kofi finally agreed to seek therapy. Now, as Kofi sits in the therapist's office, he is most afraid of losing control and being consumed by his anxiety. He hopes that with treatment, he can learn to manage his triggers and regain some sense of normalcy in his life. But for now, the smell of antiseptic still makes him feel like he's trapped in that chemical plant all over again, fighting for air.
